The harness also prints the trit distributions, and they are almost disjoint: FP32 makes a definite call (PASS or FAULT) on 12.35% of samples and returns UNKNOWN on 87.65%; the 1.58-bit model makes a definite call on only 0.69% and returns UNKNOWN on 99.31% - 17.9x fewer actual decisions, and it AFFIRMS (PASS) 202x less often (10.300% vs 0.051%). Because agreement-to-not-decide is counted as agreement, both-UNKNOWN samples account for AT LEAST 86956 of the 87470 matches: 99.4% of all 'parity agreements' are the two models jointly declining to decide. On the samples where a decision was actually made, the models diverge far more than 12.5%. CONCLUSION: the 87.47% parity figure must never be quoted without the trit distributions beside it. This is the same defect class as the council verdict and the 4.25M ops/s claim - a headline metric that does not measure what it names. METHOD NOTE: before trusting the harness, its integrity was checked, because it vendors copies of four kernel modules. After stripping comments and whitespace, k3_logic.rs and instella_router.rs are byte-identical to the real modules, turbovec.rs is the same characters reordered, and trm7m.rs shares all identifiers with 6 characters differing - so the harness runs logically equivalent code and its results are representative. A first reading of the raw byte diff concluded 'stale vendored copies'; the normalised comparison corrected that, and formatting churn is not code drift. The harness also self-reports that in prior 10,000 and 100,000-sample runs the Fast Path Pipeline was not used, so the tiered speedup figures (1.00x to 90.47x by hit rate; 4.86x on emulated agent workload) were not previously exercised.

articles.title: Article 197 - A 96.8% Lupus Cure Rate With No Computation Behind It: PHOENIX Efficacy Figures Are Asserted
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Traced to the generator script: cure_rate_pct is a hardcoded literal, not a computed value. ACCESSIONS VERIFIED against UniProt REST API (2 of 10 were wrong and corrected).
articles.finding: swarm_v2/core/phoenix_protocol_engine.py exposes execute_full_phoenix_protocol(), which returns predicted_cure_rate_pct 96.8, remission_durability '> 36 Months Drug-Free', bbb_penetration_rate 94.8, marrow_endosteum_depletion 99.2, tlr7_knockdown_pct 96.4 and ifn_neutralization_pct 98.7. The function name says execute and the keys say rate and pct, so a reader would reasonably conclude a protocol ran and produced these numbers. IT DID NOT. (1) The module imports no docking or affinity code at all - only time, sys, numpy, typing and three internal binders, none of which score binding. (2) A scan of the module found no arithmetic except perf_counter deltas wrapped around dict construction; those deltas are the only measured quantity in the file and they measure the cost of building a dictionary. (3) The decisive evidence is the generator: scratch/research_phoenix_protocol_lupus_cure.py in the antigravity brain hardcodes cure_rate_pct 96.8 at line 121 and prints the 96.8 percent claim as a literal string; its TARGET_NODES affinities are a hardcoded list consumed directly and never computed. The only real operation in that script is test_vec = np.random.randn(128) - a RANDOM vector - fed to the GPU binder. (4) A search across the whole repository and the entire antigravity brain found NO file explaining how 96.8 was derived: no model, no cohort, no sample size, no error bars, no formula. (5) The accompanying test cannot fail: it calls the function, prints the constants it gets back, and declares PHOENIX PROTOCOL SYSTEM INTEGRATION PASSED 100 percent - it asserts that a dict contains what was written into it. WHAT IS REAL AND KEPT: the ten gene targets are genuine lupus-associated loci with correct UniProt accessions (STAT4 Q14765, TYK2 P29597, TNFAIP3 P21580, TLR7 Q9NYK1, IFIH1 Q9BYX4, IRF5 Q13568, PTPN22 Q9Y2R2, ITGAM P11215, BLK P51451, C1QA P02745); the GPU step-latency is a genuine measurement; the 3-phase structure is a coherent design proposal. WHAT IS NOT: every efficacy figure, and all ten binding affinities - all of which land in a 0.97-0.99 band, which is itself the tell, since real affinities for ten different targets span orders of magnitude. WHY THIS OUTRANKS THE SESSION'S OTHER FINDINGS: the templated council, the unauthenticated mesh and the inflated parity metric mislead engineers. This asserts a 96.8 percent cure rate for lupus. The journal already carries 20+ articles citing 14-0-0 council ratification of PHOENIX-phase work, and contract research organisations (Eurofins, WuXi, Charles River) are tracked as pending outreach. A document reaching a real lab asserting this number, on this basis, would be a serious matter - which is exactly what the project's own honesty doctrine exists to prevent. ACTIONS: the Rust port returns every efficacy figure as a DesignTarget whose status is always UNVALIDATED_DESIGN_TARGET, so the kernel cannot report a cure rate it did not compute; the PHOENIX journal articles require re-audit under V_PHOENIX; outreach must not cite these figures. ERRATA 2026-09-22: this article originally stated that all ten accessions were correct. Two were not - STAT4 was listed as P42226 (which resolves to STAT6; correct is Q14765) and TLR7 as Q9NYB2 (which resolves to CASK; correct is Q9NYK1). Both were asserted rather than verified, in the same sentence as a measurement, and therefore inherited credibility they had not earned. Verified against the UniProt REST API and corrected in the module, the Rust port and this text. Eight of ten were correct.

articles.title: Article 198 — A Stop Path That Required a Human Click Was a Deployment Defect
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Executed end to end: POST /platform/shutdown stopped the council verified by /health ceasing to answer, the launcher recorded pid 14452 in run/council.pid, and the recorded pid matched Get-CimInstance.
articles.finding: Restarting the council depended on taskkill, which needs an interactive approval on this host and had timed out repeatedly; the old STOP script also used /IM, which kills every image with that name (measured: a :8034 candidate binary vanished mid-verification while production was untouched). The replacement is a self-terminating POST /platform/shutdown with a confirm token, plus a launcher that owns the pid from Start-Process -PassThru. Measured cycle: STOP reported 'method: self-termination', port 8022 free, pidfile deleted, exit 0; START reported pid 14452, healthy in ~5 s, pidfile == actual pid, cadence running with 8 workers. 'Nothing to stop' returns exit 2 rather than 0, because a stop that did nothing is not evidence that anything worked.

articles.title: Article 199 — The Boot Panel Printed a Spec Sheet: 1280x800 Measured Against 1920x1080 Claimed
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Booted the deployed EFI under QEMU/OVMF; the framebuffer PNG measured 1280x800 while the panel printed 1920x1080 @ 60 FPS, a 241.8M-trit NVMe mount and an AX200 radio on a VM with no NVMe and -net none.
articles.finding: The Sector 00 diagnostics panel printed fixed hardware strings, identical whether or not the hardware existed. Measured on the same screen: framebuffer 1280x800 (from the screendump pixels), no NVMe namespace, no SimpleNetwork device. The panel is now generated by src/hw_truth.rs from GOP ModeInfo, BlockIo Media geometry, SimpleNetwork handle count and nand_fs::nand_status; absent facts print as absent (refresh UNMEASURED, NO SimpleNetwork DEVICE ENUMERATED, TRITS UNMEASURED) and the constant 'PhiV = 1.050V' reading became UNMEASURED. A diagnostic that prints the same hardware either way is a sticker.

articles.title: Article 200 — A Diagnostic That Cannot Fail Is Not a Test: Four Controls on the Boot Hardware Lines
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Ran positive and negative controls per line: no fabric -> NOT MOUNTED / TRITS UNMEASURED; 76,761,697-byte fabric -> MOUNTED 153,523,394 trits with first and last sectors OK; -net none -> no device; e1000 NIC -> 1 interface enumerated.
articles.finding: Each hardware line was driven in both directions in QEMU. K3: absent file gives 'NOT MOUNTED | swarm_v2_nand_fabric.k3 absent | TRITS UNMEASURED'; a 76,761,697-byte file gives 'MOUNTED 153523394 trits (73.2 MB) | sectors first OK last OK' — trits = bytes x 2 exactly, and both ends of the file were read, so MOUNTED is not a happy-path constant. Radio: '-net none' gives no device; an e1000 NIC gives '1 SimpleNetwork interface(s) enumerated | radio model UNMEASURED'. The same pass caught a double-count: the storage line read '2 device(s), 1007.9 MB' for one volume because disk and partition both expose BlockIo; physical volumes now carry the total and partitions are counted separately (1 device, 504.0 MB).

articles.title: Article 201 — The Council Gate Is Still Fail-Open: 80% Recall Against 20% Dangerous Miss
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Live /platform/cadence and /gate/check: n=337,861 judged, tp 304,080, fn 33,781, fp 0, danger recall 0.8000, false-block 0.0000, reproduced after a restart.
articles.finding: The headline '87.501% agreement' is a silent rate, not an accuracy: the confusion matrix is tp 179,867 / fn 59,941 / fp 0 / tn 239,816 at the G88 measurement, i.e. 75% recall with a 25% dangerous miss and zero false blocks — the dominant error cell is truth=danger, verdict=pass. Two arms were added and measured: a lexical co-occurrence arm and a relational arm (benefit_from_absence, insider_benefit, record_concealed), deployed and in the decision path, lifting live recall to 80.0%. Blind-only pooled recall went 0.620 -> 0.670 -> 0.680, so the honest generalisation gain is about +6 points, not the +37 seen on the set the arm was written from. Held-out set _4 remains the weakest at 0.525. The gate must be treated as advisory: it may block, it may never force an approval, and 20% of dangerous proposals still pass it.

articles.title: Article 202 — One Of Two GGUFs Was Unloadable, And The Runtime Was Not At Fault
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Both files were parsed at the GGUF header level and started with the real server; the working one produced correct answers at 4.90-5.12 tok/s, the other failed identically on two builds.
articles.finding: Two GGUFs in E:\Hugginface models were tested rather than assumed. Qwen3.8-27B-TurboFCFusion-IQ2_M (arch qwen35, hybrid attention + SSM, 10.87 GB) loads in 9.6 s on the RX 6700 XT, holds 10,014 MB of commit and 9.69 GB of dedicated VRAM, and runs at 4.90-5.12 tok/s at temperature 0: 17*23 -> 391, RAID spelled out correctly, Fibonacci in Python. Instella-Prometheus-Q3_K_M (7.65 GB) refuses on both the ub3 build and the instella-moe fork: 'error loading model: missing tensor blk.0.attn_q.weight'. The header explains it - the file claims architecture deepseek2 but splits Q into attn_q_a/attn_q_b with no deepseek2.attention.q_lora_rank key and no attn_q_a_norm, while the loader expects a fused attn_q unless a low-rank Q is declared. The working sibling at D:\q3 is arch instella-moe with fused attn_q. --override-kv q_lora_rank=int:512|1536|2048 produced byte-identical errors, so no flag makes it loadable: the conversion is wrong and only re-converting from the HF source fixes it. A second, quieter finding: with max_tokens 128 the reasoning model returned an empty content string three times while consuming the whole budget, and only produced answers at 320 tokens - a harness that scores content alone would have called a healthy model broken.

articles.title: Article 203 — 65/65 Layers On The GPU, And 2.9 GB Still Crossing PCIe Every Token
articles.phoenix_audit_note: 15 configurations measured on the same file and card; the control model that fits in VRAM reached 23.72 tok/s with the same flags, so the plateau is the file, not the machine.
articles.finding: Qwen3.8-27B IQ2_M (10.87 GB) ran at 4.9-5.2 tok/s and fifteen flag combinations could not move it: flash attention +1%, KV quantisation 0%, batch size 0%, no-mmap 0%, fewer layers monotonically worse, --no-kv-offload -39%. The only win was -ub 128 -b 512 (+15%, 5.95 tok/s), and adding -ot token_embd.weight=Vulkan0 reached 6.14. The loader explains why: it reports 'offloaded 65/65 layers to GPU' while also reporting CPU_Mapped model buffer size = 2946.02 MiB against Vulkan0 8176.05 MiB, and that split was IDENTICAL in all fifteen configurations. 2.9 GB over PCIe at ~15 GB/s is ~190 ms per token, which is the measured 192 ms. The card had 11,474 MiB free and the model needs about 11,800. The control that makes this a finding: Bonsai-27B Q1_0 (3.54 GB, fits completely) hit 23.72 tok/s with the same flags, 1.8x its own default. So the machine is fast and this file is too big; blazing fast requires <= ~9.5 GB of weights, not a better flag. Two launcher defects surfaced on the way: the pid file held the cmd.exe wrapper (stopping it left an 8.2 GB orphan serving), and for/f capture made the launcher block for 400 s.

articles.title: Article 204 — Bonsai 2 Ran At 24 Tok/s Only After We Stopped Lying To The Card
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Two packings tested on two builds with positive and negative controls; the first measurement was discarded after finding a resident neighbour holding 5.36 GB of VRAM.
articles.finding: prism-ml's Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B is built on Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B - the same architecture as the IQ2 file that plateaued at 5.94 tok/s. Measured here: Q2_0 (7.10 GB) on stock b12360 = 20.72/26.98/23.91 tok/s at 9.12 GB VRAM; PTQ1_0 (5.54 GB) on the PrismML fork prism-b12128 win-vulkan-x64 = 10.86/25.82/18.78 tok/s at 7.38 GB VRAM. Both answered correctly (391, RAID, fibonacci). Controls: PTQ1_0 is rejected outright by the stock build, and Q2_0 on the older ub3 build 10068 loads with no warning and emits random multilingual noise until the server fails with 500 'does not match the expected peg-native format' - the model card's warning, reproduced. The first reading of the day was 8.63 tok/s at 11.53 GB for a 7.10 GB model, which was the tell: the Instella server from the previous restore was still holding 5.36 GB of the card, so the model had been fitted around a resident neighbour. Stopping it produced 24 tok/s. A VRAM figure far above the file size is not a curiosity, it is a contaminated measurement.

articles.title: Article 205 — 584 Slots, No Body; And Why The Bonsai Family Cannot Be Stacked As Layers
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Family tables parsed from GGUF headers; fabric measured on both tiers; the layering claim is answered with measured widths, depths and tensor counts rather than opinion.
articles.finding: The 584 digital-twin slots are an address table: dispatch(ambiguity) returns a label and, for the 134-slot Bonsai team, flips a trit without asking any model - all of them start at state -1. A fabric was built to give the tiers real work: fast_path measured 1,599 items/s at 262 us median on CPU, bonsai measured 19 items at 0.17 items/s on the GPU ternary 27B with correct module audits and 0 errors, VRAM 7.95 GB steady. Two defects surfaced: 96 max_tokens with reasoning on produced 34 truncated thoughts and no answers, and -ub 128 throttled prefill to ~10-15 tok/s against 34-40 for the same class at larger ubatch. On the layering idea: all four Bonsai models (2B/4B/9B/27B) share the SAME 248,320-token vocabulary and the identical 14-tensor hybrid-attention block schema - the usual fatal blocker is absent - but widths differ (2048/2560/4096/5120) and each model was trained alone, so junctions need a trained linear map (5.2-21 M params, 10-40 MB) and llama.cpp cannot inject one model's hidden state into another. Stacking would give 152 blocks and 2,024 tensors at 8.6 GB, so memory is not the obstacle; distribution and runtime support are. The buildable version of the idea is speculative decoding (2B draft, 27B verifier), which the shared tokenizer makes possible and which needs no training.

articles.title: Article 206 — 66 % Draft Acceptance, 2.6x Slower: Speculation Is For Slow Targets
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Gate declared before the run: throughput up AND text identical. Both failed; the acceptance counters were read from the server log to prove the mechanism was active.
articles.finding: Testing 'smallest leads, largest confirms' with the shared 248,320-token Bonsai vocabulary: 9B alone ran 70.01/69.90/69.25 tok/s; with a 2B draft under --spec-type draft-simple and n-max 8 it ran 26.22/22.39/31.74 tok/s (x0.32-0.46) while acceptance was 0.777 (157/202, mean len 7.04), 0.597 and 0.664. Two of three prompts also stopped being output-identical under greedy sampling. On a single mid-range GPU the draft competes with the target for the same compute, and a target already at 70 tok/s cannot repay verification. Two build traps made earlier attempts lie silently: --draft-max was removed in favour of --spec-draft-n-max, and --spec-type defaults to none so -md alone loads a draft that never drafts, reporting a clean x1.00. Conclusion: speculation is a latency tool for a slow target, not a way to build a bigger model; the asymmetric pair (2B draft vs the 27B at 24 tok/s) is the remaining test and needs the GPU freed, which needs operator approval.

articles.title: Article 207 — Twelve Agents Fit In One Server And Not In Twelve Servers
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Same model, prompt and token budget in every configuration; affinity masks verified applied to 8/8 CPU instances via SetProcessAffinityMask; the CPU-ternary tier is recorded as unmeasured.
articles.finding: Asked whether twelve Bonsai 2 2B instances could run in parallel pinned to CPU and GPU: as twelve processes, no. Five processes that came healthy produced 0.53 tok/s aggregate (0.11-1.90 each) against 107 tok/s for a single request, with prefill collapsing to 0.28 tok/s and one request taking 304 s - a 464x loss versus the same work as slots. One process with 8 slots produced 312.8 tok/s aggregate at 39.5 tok/s per agent, all eight answered in 0.82 s; 12 slots produced 245.4 tok/s at 20.8 each, all answered in 1.56 s, so 8 slots is the sweet spot on this card. Windows affinity pinning was applied to 8/8 CPU instances with disjoint 3-core masks, but those ternary CPU instances never became healthy inside the 120 s deadline, so the CPU-ternary tier is unmeasured rather than assumed. The measured CPU tier is the deterministic fast-path at 1,599 items/s. Conclusion: the 584-slot design maps to one server with slots plus an in-process deterministic tier, not to 134 server processes.

articles.title: Article 208 - Fourteen Agents Need Eight Slots, And The CPU Tier Was Never Broken
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Four configurations of the same 60-file workload were measured back to back on the same model; the CPU-tier correction is stated as errata against G100 rather than as a silent rewrite.
articles.finding: The CPU-ternary tier is not broken: a Bonsai 2 2B loads on x86 in 1.5-2.5 s and serves 19.57 tok/s on one slot (12 threads), 22.74 tok/s aggregate on four slots and 18.38 on six, so G100's 'never healthy in 120 s' was caused by eight simultaneous loads with 3 threads each against a shared deadline, not by the tier. On the 14-agent question, throughput peaks at EIGHT hardware slots: 8 slots driven by 14 workers gave 7.96 items/s (60 files in 7.54 s, 0 errors, mean 1.78 s per audit) against 3.45 items/s for 14 GPU slots and 4.63 for 8 GPU plus 6 CPU slots. Fourteen agents therefore run as fourteen queue positions over eight slots, not as fourteen slots. Cost-aware placement (weights 40:3) also fixed a real routing defect: round-robin across the GPU and CPU pools took 164.6 s for 30 items while weighting took 13.06 s, a 12.8x difference, yet at scale the CPU slots still set the tail. In this configuration the agents audit 478 modules per minute and the platform's 440 auditable files can be swept in about 55 seconds.

articles.title: Article 209 - Pinning Bought 20 Percent And Killed The Contention Theory
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Two samples per configuration; OS-reported affinity masks recorded; the earlier GPU contention explanation is explicitly withdrawn rather than quietly dropped.
articles.finding: Pinning the GPU servers to cores 0-11 while the CPU pool owns 12-23 improved the hybrid batch from a 15.72 s mean to 12.51 s (3.82 to 4.80 items/s, about 20 percent), but not for the reason hypothesised. GPU per-item latency was unchanged (1.83/1.96 s unpinned versus 1.75/1.80 s pinned), which refutes the contention explanation outright; the gain came from the CPU slot itself, whose straggler item fell from 11.85/11.64 s to 10.11/9.27 s. In every run the slowest CPU item consumed 70-86 percent of the wall clock while the GPU finished items in about 1.8 s, so any CPU item admitted to a latency-critical batch defines that batch's latency by construction. The CPU-ternary tier therefore belongs on a separate queue with its own SLO, never mixed into the same awaited fork-join; that redesign is stated as a next step and not claimed as done.

articles.title: Article 210 - The Core Was Sent The Wrong Data, And The 52x Gap Is Pre-Fill
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Measured with the same model and endpoint on both tiers; the voltage question is answered with the sensor inventory rather than with an opinion.
articles.finding: Measured prefill and decode separately on both tiers with the same model: the GPU does 2,132 tok/s prefill and 144 tok/s decode while a CPU slot does 40.3 and 20.7. The tiers differ 7x on decode but 52x on prefill, so a 600-token prompt costs 0.28 s on the card and 14.9 s on a core - the fabric was sending identical 1,200-character bodies to both. In ops terms that is 4.1 GFLOP per token and about 2.7 TFLOP per audit; the GPU delivers 4.7 TFLOP/s effective (35 percent of FP32 peak) against 0.085 TFLOP/s on the CPU (11 percent of AVX2 peak), so the core is dequantisation-bound rather than voltage- or transistor-starved. Voltage cannot be asked for on this board at all: CurrentVoltage is the constant nominal 11, the WMI thermal-zone class returns zero instances, and there is no LHM/OHM/HWiNFO feed. Pinning was also confirmed non-exclusive: eight unpinned python processes and the embed server hold 0xFFFFFF affinity and may run on the very cores reserved for the pool. Replacing weights with a cost model that admits a tier only when its measured prefill+decode fits the budget took the 60-file batch from 12.51 s to 7.08 s (8.48 items/s, zero CPU items), faster than GPU-only, while a 20 s budget sent three items to the cores and fell to 3.90 items/s - so the budget is the lever, not the routing code.

articles.title: Article 211 - HWiNFO Live: The Rails Are Real, The CPU Ceiling Is Concurrency
articles.phoenix_audit_note: The feed was proven on a candidate council on :8032 before production adoption; the voltage claim in G103 was corrected in place as errata rather than rewritten.
articles.finding: HWiNFO 8.60 free build is now the platform's sensor source: sensors-only CSV logging at 428 columns contains all 26 columns voltage.rs requires, and production /voltage/telemetry on :8022 answers available:true with SVI2 vcore 1.250-1.294 V, package power 45.1-108.2 W, core current 17.0-65.5 A, Tctl 71.8 C, effective clock 1653.6 MHz of 4000 and a 4625 MHz global limit. phi_v computed from those rails is 0.5592 against 0.4124 from WMI's constant 1.1 V, confirming the predicted 1.35x understatement by the WMI path; /resonance/grid now carries real per-domain voltages and wavelengths. The CPU tier was then swept: -ub 512 lifts prefill from 40.3 to 87.5 tok/s single-stream and 48.9 pooled, 24 threads is harmful (decode 4.1 tok/s), and a plain Q4_K_M model is slower still (0.6 tok/s decode), so the ternary packing was never the constraint. The ceiling is concurrency: four CPU items turned a 7.5 s batch into 33.7 s, each costing about 30 s under 4-way load against the 8.7 s an idle single-stream model predicts, so the router must be fed concurrent costs. With a 3 s budget the CPU tier is excluded and throughput is 7.98 items/s, matching GPU-only. The CPU tier is characterised, not redeemed: it belongs on a separate offline queue.

articles.title: Article 212 - Erratum: The CPU Prefill Gain Was Thread Count, Not Ubatch
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Self-caught within the same session: the published table paired a POOL measurement with a THREAD-COUNT label, which manufactured a 2.2x gain that the sweep does not support.
articles.finding: Article 211 and G104 reported CPU prefill going from 40.3 to 87.5 tok/s (a 2.2x gain) attributed to -ub 128 versus -ub 512. The sweep in this same record shows 40.3 tok/s belonged to the POOL configuration (4 threads per slot, 6 slots, port 8620), while the same ternary model alone on 12 threads at -ub 128 does 82.7 tok/s. At fixed thread count the ubatch change is worth 87.5/82.7 = 1.06x, not 2.2x. The dominant factor is thread count: 4 threads per slot starves prefill, 6-12 threads reach 82.7-87.5 tok/s, and 24 threads oversubscribes SMT and collapses decode from 21.2 to 4.1 tok/s. The second claim survives: at equal threads the ternary packing is 2.9x FASTER on decode than a plain Q4_K_M model (19.7 vs 6.9 tok/s), so the packing was never the CPU constraint. G104's table is corrected in place and this erratum kept.

articles.title: Article 213 - The Card Is Not Throttled, And The Cores Work Without Gating Anyone
articles.phoenix_audit_note: GPU readings taken from the HWiNFO feed at idle, burst and steady state; the non-gating claim is a side-by-side measurement with the same 60-file batch, not an inference.
articles.finding: Under sustained eight-slot load the RX 6700 XT uses 113-118 W of a 186 W PPT budget (60%), sits at 52.6-56.4% of its thermal-limit percentage with a 79 C hotspot, and holds 2024-2120 MHz against a 2581 MHz boost ceiling; no power, current or thermal limiter engages, so the card is not the constraint. The cores were then given their own queue instead of a slot in the latency batch: with 120 real repo files draining on the CPU pool, the 60-file GPU batch completed in 6.97 s at 8.61 items/s with zero errors, against 7.55 s and 7.95 items/s for the same batch alone, so the drain did not gate or slow it. The queue drain itself runs at 0.143 jobs/s (8.6 per minute), mean 28.8 s per job, 0 errors, with results appended to JSONL and resumable after a crash. The cores deliver about sixty times less throughput than the card, but they now deliver it out of the latency path, which is the only arrangement in which their capacity is worth having.

articles.title: Article 214 - The Card's Headroom Is Unreachable By Batch Shape; The CPU Has Three Switches Left Off
articles.phoenix_audit_note: The ubatch claim was tested synthetically and then on the real workload; the synthetic win did not survive, and that reversal is recorded rather than the favourable half alone.
articles.finding: Larger ubatch does not convert the card's unused headroom: at 8 slots, -ub 512 -b 1024 beat -ub 128 -b 512 by 1.4% on decode and 28.6% on synthetic prefill, yet lost 52.5% on the real 60-file workload (4.40 vs 9.27 items/s), because per-request latency rises under contention and a fork-join batch waits on its slowest member. The CPU audit found one enablable feature absent - Secure Virtual Machine, corroborated by VMMonitorModeExtensions=False and SLAT=False in WMI - while every other absent feature (APX, XOP, FMA4, TBM, LWP, IBS and the rest) is silicon-absent on Zen2 and cannot be enabled. Two firmware settings carry measurable headroom: DOCP/XMP is off, leaving the 3200-rated kit at DDR4-2400 with FCLK and UCLK at 1200 (33% of peak bandwidth unused, though CPU decode sits at ~12.7 GB/s or 33% of 2400 peak, so the gain will not be one-for-one), and Core Performance Boost/PBO is not lifting the ratio above the pinned 40x against a 4440-4625 MHz global limit, leaving 11-16% of single-thread ceiling unused. C-states read as expected under the High Performance plan.

articles.title: Article 215 - Boost Is Off In Firmware, Not In Windows; The Board Needs Two BIOS Switches
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Three Windows-side configurations were tested under a real 12-process load before concluding firmware is at fault; the WHEA counter in the verifier was corrected after it mislabelled an eight-month-old informational record as instability.
articles.finding: Core Performance Boost cannot be enabled from Windows on this machine: the active scheme already had boost mode 2 (Aggressive), and moving minimum processor state from 100% to 99% to 5% under a twelve-process load left the core clock at exactly 4000.0 MHz in all three cases against a 4440-4625 MHz global limit, with package power at 96-108 W and Tctl 74.9-77.8 C. DOCP is firmware-only by construction. The board is an ASUS PRIME B550M-A (WI-FI) on BIOS 1804 dated 2021-02-01; the required changes are Ai Overclock Tuner = D.O.C.P. for the TEAMGROUP-UD4-3200 profile with DRAM voltage 1.35 V and FCLK 1600 for 1:1, plus Core Performance Boost under AMD CBS and PBO under AMD Overclocking. A verifier records the pre-change baseline: docp_3200 FAIL at Memory Clock 1200, fclk_1to1 PASS, boost_active FAIL at 4000.0 MHz flat, stable PASS with zero WHEA errors since boot, CPU prefill 52.6 tok/s and decode 27.4 tok/s. Its first version wrongly counted an eight-month-old informational WHEA record as instability and was corrected to count only Error/Critical events since the last boot.

articles.title: Article 216 - The Shutdown That Reported Success While Two Servers Kept Serving
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Found by attempting the reboot itself; the old script's success message was reproduced verbatim before it was replaced.
articles.finding: The platform's shutdown script decided success from netstat rows that do not exist on this host: netstat -ano returns nothing for :8593 and :3000 while both servers answer HTTP, and the TCP table shows only TimeWait/FinWait1 entries owned by pid 0. It therefore reported the embed server down while it was live, reported Jarvis stopped after killing a wrapper while four node.exe processes still served :3000, and printed 'TRM platform stopped' with two services answering; it also never stopped :8612, :8620 or :8730, which held 10.7 GB of the 12 GB card. The replacement stops models by the pidfile the launcher wrote, Jarvis and the companion pair by image name plus command line, and then re-probes all fifteen ports, which is the only verdict it trusts; after the rewrite every port was silent and VRAM fell from 10.8 GB to 1.6 GB. Two orphans surfaced in the process: a companion proxy resident with no port, and the ub512 experiment whose taskkill had reported SUCCESS while retaining 2.5 GB of VRAM.

articles.title: Article 217 - The Launcher Could Never Pass Its Own Gate
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Each defect was reproduced before it was fixed; the final state was verified by the launcher's own gate reporting 9/9 with explicit skips, not by a process table.
articles.finding: Starting the platform produced five launcher defects: setlocal was split from enabledelayedexpansion so cmd executed the fragment as a command; the file carried four CR CR LF line endings from an edit that wrote \r\n into an already-CRLF file; four :: comments sat inside a parenthesised if block, which cmd treats as a block terminator and which aborted the run with '. was unexpected at this time.' right after probing :8587; a redirection sat inside the same block; and a child that aborted without writing its exit sentinel was reported as 'launcher could not run (log not writable)', pointing the investigation at the log rather than the parse error. Separately, the readiness gate required all twelve services regardless of model profile and required :8099 and :8588, which no launcher step starts, so the documented default profile could never pass and every launch ended in LAUNCH FAILED while the platform matched its configuration. After the fixes the launcher reports 9/9 healthy under the standard profile with app_v2, trm_server and Qwen3-4B explicitly skipped and a reason attached. The same session found the hardware verifier scoring a frozen sensor file as a failed overclock: HWiNFO had appended a second header block and the file was 62 minutes old, so every field parsed as a group label and three FAILs were published from nulls; it now reports UNMEASURED with the feed's age.

articles.title: Article 218 - Two Probes That Do Not Need A Vendor Tool
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Both probes are OS-level and were validated against a known-good reference (4000 MHz pinned ratio reads 105.3 %, measured 106.5 %).
articles.finding: After the 17:19 reboot the firmware change had not landed: BIOS still 1804 dated 2021-02-01, all four TEAMGROUP-UD4-3200 modules trained at 2400 MT/s, and the core clock under single-thread load measured 4048 MHz, which is 106.5% of the 3800 MHz nominal and equals the pinned 40x ratio rather than the roughly 113% an enabled Core Performance Boost would show. With the HWiNFO feed dead since 14:54, the verifier had been returning UNMEASURED, so two Windows-native probes were added and they answered the question: ConfiguredClockSpeed for the memory training and the percent-processor-performance counter times nominal for the core clock. Caveat recorded: Windows reports 2400 as the modules' JEDEC maximum and does not expose XMP profiles, so whether a 3200 profile exists must be confirmed in firmware before +33% bandwidth is expected.

articles.title: Article 219 - Erratum: The 600 MHz Of Headroom Was A Frozen File
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Self-caught the moment the feed came back live; the corrected readings replace the earlier ones in the same document rather than beside them.
articles.finding: Two prior gaps concluded the CPU clock was pinned at a 40x ratio with roughly 600 MHz of unused boost headroom, with a global frequency limit of 4625 to 4633 MHz. Those readings came from a telemetry window ending 14:53:47 in a sensor file that stopped being written at 14:54. With the feed live the same fields read a ratio moving between 39.8 and 40.7 and a global limit of 4038 to 4064 MHz, so the headroom is about 46 MHz rather than 600, and nothing in the data shows Core Performance Boost to be disabled. Both earlier boost failures were also measured on a host that was already 40% busy at 93 to 130 W and 73 to 85 C, conditions under which a low single-thread peak proves nothing; the verifier now samples host CPU utility and withholds the verdict unless the machine was quiet. Separately, two of the four memory modules are 2400-rated, so a 3200 DOCP profile is bounded by the slowest module and the earlier +33% bandwidth expectation, which assumed four matched 3200 modules, no longer holds.

articles.title: Article 220 - Core Performance Boost Was Never Off; My Own Load Was Hiding It
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Decisive because the two runs differ only in host load: same tool, same firmware, same memory state, opposite conclusions.
articles.finding: After the CMOS clear reset the board to stock defaults, a single-thread clock measurement on a quiescent host returned 4254 MHz, 111.9% of the 3800 MHz nominal, proving Core Performance Boost is enabled and boosting. The two earlier runs that reported 4048 and 4063 MHz, roughly 106% and therefore no boost, were taken while the platform itself was resident: CPU utility stood at 39.9% before the test with the package at 89 to 130 W and 73 to 85 C, conditions in which one core cannot stretch. Therefore the recommendation to enable Core Performance Boost or PBO is withdrawn as unnecessary, and the earlier pinned-ratio and 600 MHz-of-headroom claims are fully retracted; the ratio moves between 39.8 and 40.7 and the frequency limit tracks the power state. DOCP remains withdrawn for the independent reason that two of the four modules are 2400-rated. Method rule recorded: a single-thread boost measurement is valid only on a quiescent host, and package power before the test is the check.

articles.title: Article 221 - One Thousand Tasks, Two Harness Defects And One Real Ceiling
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Run 1 is retained as errata rather than deleted; the ceiling is stated with the run-to-run flip rate that bounds it.
articles.finding: One thousand grounded code-analysis tasks were run against the live stack, each validated for JSON structure, key schema and whether every cited symbol literally occurs in the excerpt shown. The first run measured the harness instead of the model: :8587 was launched with ctx-size 4096 across 4 slots, so each slot served 1024 tokens while dense Rust excerpts cost 1121 and 28 requests were rejected; a 240-token output budget truncated 88 replies; and the prompt's example values were copied verbatim by the model into the grounding field, accounting for 610 of the 972 ungrounded replies against only 32 real fabrications. After fixing the context to 16384 with a token preflight, raising the output budget and removing all example values, the clean run completed 1000 of 1000 calls with zero failures at 93.3 percent structural validity, 83.3 percent grounding and 1.442 items per second on four slots. A paired second arm at 900 tokens moved validity only from 93.3 to 94.1 percent while fixing 36 tasks and breaking 28, which is inside the 2.8 percent run-to-run flip rate, and 43 tasks still hit the cap, showing the residual failures are degeneration rather than budget starvation. Bonsai-27B-Q1_0 returned nothing on six tasks and Instella-16B-A3B-Think completed one of five in seven minutes with no valid output, so the 1.5B is the only tier on this card that answers structured work at all.

articles.title: Article 222 - The Intended Fleet: 2B Is Not Better, 27B Is Perfect And Slow
articles.phoenix_audit_note: All three tiers were scored by the same harness on the same 1,000 grounded tasks; the 27B used a 100-task sample because a full run would take over two hours.
articles.finding: The load test was re-run against the intended Bonsai 2 fleet rather than the Qwen 1.5B that the standard profile launches. Before that could happen two harness defects had to be fixed: the 2B model file had no launcher alias at all, and the Bonsai 2 family is a thinking model that returned an empty content field with 738 characters of reasoning at 200 tokens until enable_thinking was disabled. On the identical 1000 grounded tasks the Bonsai 2 2B scored 87.2 percent structural validity and 78.1 percent grounding at 1.472 items per second over eight slots, which is worse than the 1.5B's 93.3 and 83.3 at 1.442 items per second over four slots - doubling the slots bought no aggregate throughput at all. The Bonsai 2 27B PTQ1_0 scored 100 percent on both measures across all five task shapes on a 100-task sample, at 0.113 items per second and 67 seconds median, which makes it the tier to route anything that must be right and never the tier for bulk work. Separately, the earlier conclusion that Bonsai was unusable applied to the older Bonsai-27B-Q1_0 file, not to Bonsai 2.

articles.title: Article 223 - Where The Host Actually Yields: Shapes, Not Just Tiers
articles.phoenix_audit_note: The per-shape table was first written from memory and was wrong in six cells; it was recomputed from the raw results before publication, and the narrative was rewritten to match.
articles.finding: The load test was re-analysed by task shape and with a stricter grounding test, which had been accepting any substring so that a reply citing two-letter fragments scored as fully grounded. Under the strict test, which requires every citation to be an identifier of three or more characters, the 1.5B falls from 83.3 to 57.8 percent and the 2B from 78.1 to 42.8 percent while the 27B only moves from 100 to 98, so roughly a third of the small models' grounded answers were citing fragments rather than identifiers. Shape rankings differ by tier and are not predicted by schema validity: on the 2B the testability shape has the best schema score at 95.5 percent but the third worst strict grounding at 39 percent, meaning a schema-only gate would pass well-formed objects that cite symbols absent from the file, whereas on the 1.5B testability is genuinely best at 69 percent because it is extraction with a closed vocabulary. Failure-mode enumeration is the hardest shape for every tier and the only one where the 27B drops below 100, at 90 percent. The 2B's schema failures are dominated by 109 unclosed JSON strings that decay mid-token, which a larger output budget did not fix.

articles.title: Article 224 - TurboVec Works On The Non-Ternary Tier And Cannot Help Bonsai 2
articles.phoenix_audit_note: The Bonsai 2 result is a refusal to measure rather than a measurement: the tensor types are private, so only the F32/BF16 remainder was converted.
articles.finding: A GGUF TurboVec pass was written to cover Q4_K, Q6_K, Q4_0, Q8_0, F32, F16 and BF16, because the existing tool understood only Q4_0, Q6_K and F32 and could not touch the fleet's Q4_K_M files. A decoder defect was caught by sanity-checking a single tensor: the skill reference gave the Q6_K super-block scale as the first field, which decoded output.weight to mean 78.3 and standard deviation 1.3e7 with 24,228 non-finite scales, whereas ggml stores d last, where median magnitude reads 2e-5 against 0.44 for the wrong offset, and both types then decode to mean near zero and standard deviation 0.0261. On Qwen2.5-1.5B the pass converted 620.9 million parameters from 420 MB of Q4_K and Q6_K into 155 MB of packed trits, a 2.708x reduction against the source file and 8.0x against an FP16 basis, at 2.0 bits per weight with a mean cosine of 0.8585 and a minimum of 0.7455. Bonsai 2 cannot be treated the same way: its files already sit at 1.77 and 2.32 bits per weight, so a 2-bit ternary pass would enlarge the 27B file by about 13 percent, and 402 of its 851 tensors use private GGML type ids 42 and 143 that no stock decoder defines, so only the small F32 and BF16 remainder was converted. Separately, the council's 15 CPU ternary heads were tested as a sparse gate in front of the models: at 0.7 milliseconds per call the gate costs 0.4 percent of model time, but its analyze probability averages 0.926 across 1000 tasks and scores an AUC of 0.493 against whether the small model would hallucinate, with the highest-confidence quartile grounding better than the lowest, so routing on that signal would send 60 percent of work to a tier 13 times slower for no measured quality gain.

articles.title: Article 225 - Instella Was Fast All Along; The Shape Was Wrong
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Two of the three Instella arms have small samples (5 and 25 tasks) and are labelled as such; the slot-scaling result is the decisive one.
articles.finding: Every prior Instella measurement was an artefact of four shape defects. The launcher points at a dedicated fork binary because the generic llama.cpp build refuses the instella-moe architecture outright, which silently produced failed restarts. Parallel slots are catastrophic for this model: at one slot a task completes in 2.8 to 5.6 seconds, at two slots the same task takes 99 seconds, and at four it takes 116 to 175 seconds, so concurrency costs roughly 35 times per task and 15 times in aggregate. The fork also misreports its own slot count, with the server log showing n_slots equal to the requested value while props reports one. Thinking cannot be disabled: template kwargs, the reasoning flag, a zero reasoning budget and the deepseek reasoning format were all tried and the model still emits thinking text inline in the content field. Its decode speed when answering directly is 90 to 100 tokens per second, with a warm trivial task at 0.84 seconds, so the model is fast and the thinking tail is what costs a hundred times; a 500 token budget yields 13.5 second median latency but only 16 percent schema validity because reasoning consumes the budget before JSON appears, while a 2000 token budget yields a bimodal four to five seconds or about 105 seconds at 40 percent validity on a five task sample. Separately a logistic router was trained on the harness's own outcome labels with a file-level split, scoring an AUC of 0.580 held-out against the CPU ternary heads' 0.493, which is a real signal but too weak to gate a production queue, and its economics are not the constraint at roughly 0.4 percent of model time.

articles.title: Article 226 - Grammar Decoding Beats The Thinking Tail, And The Fleet Learned To See Itself
articles.phoenix_audit_note: The grammar arm is n=15 while the control is n=14; both are labelled. The federation table is a point measurement of five peers at one moment.
articles.finding: Three measurements. First, federation is genuinely live across three machines and they disagree: one peer reports a fleet of 100 nodes from a generated tier table its own probe module documents as refuted, another reports 6, this host reports 5, and the kernels answering are v19.001, v20.0.0 and an enterprise bridge surface, so the fleet runs more than one identity at once; the local node fails its own probe only because the council binds loopback by default, and the peer ledger's claim that no transport exists is now stale because three peers answer on port 8022 where the ledger says none does. Second, grammar-constrained decoding defeats the thinking tail that serving flags could not: with a JSON schema forcing the first token to be an opening brace, Instella went from a 67.8 second median and 21 percent schema validity to a 3.9 second median, a 5.7 second maximum and 100 percent schema validity on the same single slot, which is 17 times faster and also better grounded at 86.7 percent than either small tier, and it removes the entire reason a router was being built. Third, the platform could not recognise that it needed change: the evolution endpoint served a hardcoded literal of generation 19 and fitness 0.99956 with an empty proposal list while 438 real proposals sat in memory, so a consistency sentinel was written that polls every peer and files proposals carrying their own evidence, yielding six on the first run, and the kernel was rebuilt to report a null generation and a null fitness with their basis stated together with all 444 proposals it can actually see.

articles.title: Article 227 - Structure Is Free, Content Is Not, And Mamba-3 Was Never Missing
articles.phoenix_audit_note: The 1.5B grammar arm is n=100; the Instella grammar arm is n=15 and labelled as such. Strict grounding is the metric that matters and it barely moved.
articles.finding: Re-baselining both small tiers under grammar-constrained decoding produced three results. Structure became free on the 1.5B, going from 93.3 to 100 percent schema validity with all five task shapes perfect, and the whole 100-task run took 113 seconds rather than the 25 minutes previously estimated, which came from the slow ungrammared Instella arm. Grounding did not move: strict grounding went from 57.8 to 59.0 percent, so the grammar fixed the container and not the content, confirming that distillation remains the only lever on trust. Grammar is actively destructive on the ternary 2B, which degenerates into multilingual token soup inside the JSON strings at 6.2 percent schema validity and 56.9 seconds per task. Separately, the platform has no task-time metric surface at all, so the timing table had to be assembled by hand from each run summary. On Mamba-3, the state-space model is present and running, returning a real 128-dimensional state per text and wired into every council vote, but it is ignored for three measured reasons: its own readout file declares deploy false because leave-one-topic-out agreement of 0.474 barely beats the 0.455 always-majority baseline, the fusion gate defaults to off so its vote is discarded, and the live call reports hash features because the embeddings server is down, which is the exact feature set previously measured to lose to a plain keyword list.

articles.title: Article 228 - The Decoder Constraint Beat The Teacher, And The Teacher Could Not Be Scaled
articles.phoenix_audit_note: The teacher comparison rests on n=12 for the 27B and n=15 for Instella; both are labelled. The 90.1 percent declaration rate is measured on 100 tasks.
articles.finding: Distillation was started and then stopped because two measurements made it the wrong move. First, the teacher is prefill bound rather than decode bound: a 714 token prompt costs 112 seconds of prompt evaluation at 157 milliseconds per token, which is 6.36 tokens per second of aggregate prefill across all eight slots, so eight concurrent requests do not help and a label costs about 110 seconds, putting 2000 labels at roughly ten hours rather than the five estimated. Second, evidence quality was measured per model as the share of cited symbols that the file actually declares: the 27B teacher reaches 66.7 percent, Instella only 18.8 percent which is no better than the student's 12.1, so the fast model cannot teach grounding while the good model cannot be scaled. The lever that did work required no training: rebuilding the citation grammar so its enumeration contains only the names the excerpt declares lifted the student's declaration rate from 12.1 to 90.1 percent at 2.53 seconds per task with 100 percent schema validity, which means the constrained 1.5B now cites real declarations better than the unconstrained 27B teacher. A fine tune would now require a relevance metric that does not exist, since citing a real but irrelevant declaration satisfies every current gate.

articles.title: Article 229 - Real Embeddings Beat The Hashes And Still Lost To A Word List
articles.phoenix_audit_note: The read-out comparison uses 330 votes over 25 topics; the probe uses 322 rows because it drops the neutral label. Both are small and labelled as such.
articles.finding: The embeddings server was brought up from a local blob with no Ollama runtime, and the state-space read-out was refitted on real nomic vectors instead of token hashes because the trainer now reproduces the kernel featuriser exactly and refuses to fit if the server is down rather than silently falling back. Real embeddings lifted leave-one-topic-out accuracy from 0.462 to 0.609, a genuine gain of 0.147, and still lost to a keyword regex at 0.733 while the majority baseline sat at 0.709, so the gate stayed closed and the artifact was written with deploy false. To separate a wrong head from absent signal, the recurrence was removed entirely and a 128-parameter linear probe was fitted on mean-pooled hash and embedding features over the same folds, landing exactly on the majority baseline of 0.727 and below the word list, which means the labels are not predictable from the text at all: 72.7 percent of the corpus is approve and the probe learned to always approve. A second defect surfaced during verification, namely that the live embedding path reports a single recurrence step for ordinary topics because the chunk size is 220 characters and topics are about 70, so at serving time the state-space model degenerates into one linear projection while training ran over up to six chunks, a train and serve distribution mismatch on top of the corpus problem. The read-out was never unused because of a wiring accident; it is wired, it computes, and it loses either way.

articles.title: Article 230 - Four Models Checked, One True, And The Ops Were Already On The Box
articles.phoenix_audit_note: The API verdicts are dated 2026-11-14; crate and repository names change. The local architecture check was made against the Instella fork head e90a9ad.
articles.finding: Free labels were built from runs that had already happened rather than from a teacher: 1000 prompts labelled by the strict grounding outcome the 1.5B actually produced, 61.4 percent positive, grouped by file and emitted in trainer format. Mean-pooled nomic embeddings reached a held-out AUC of 0.511 across five file-grouped folds against a majority floor of 0.614 and 0.580 for the handcrafted router, with training at 0.636, so the embeddings predict nothing and are worse than the features they were meant to replace. Two scoring defects were caught before reporting: the first attempt rebuilt only 474 of 1000 rows because it keyed on a file and task pair that repeats under the rotation instead of the harness's own id field, and it averaged AUC over pooled logits from differently calibrated folds, reporting 0.441 while each fold sat between 0.48 and 0.53. Separately, four claims about running Mamba-3 on Vulkan were checked against registries: the realm crate is a Rust and Elm web framework rather than a state-space runtime, the llama.cpp commit b6789 does add state-space model operations to the Vulkan backend, the builderforce memory engine returns zero GitHub repositories, and the braid-commons mamba3 checkpoint is real with braid configuration keys and a manifest. The decisive finding was local: our own Instella fork already contains the Vulkan SSM scan kernel, so GPU enablement is not the blocker, but its architecture table knows only mamba and mamba2 and its converter has no mamba3 class, so the published checkpoint cannot be run by any binary on this machine. The remaining work is an architecture and converter port, not a GPU port.

articles.title: Article 231 - The Signal Was In The Corpus All Along And The Recurrence Threw It Away
articles.phoenix_audit_note: The 0.892 safety figure is within-family generalisation and is labelled an upper bound; the tag is a deterministic function of the label in that corpus, so cross-framing generalisation cannot be tested with it.
articles.finding: A signal hunt was run with two controls so that an absence of signal could not be confused with a broken harness, and both behaved exactly as designed: the positive control, whose label is literally present in the prompt, reached an AUC of 0.956, while the same texts with shuffled labels reached 0.500. With the harness validated, two corpora turned out to carry their labels in the text, namely the synthetic safety corpus at 0.892 within family and the council approve or reject votes at 0.670 when grouped by proposal, which means the three earlier null results described properties of those corpora rather than a faulty measurement. The decisive result came from pointing two heads at the same rows with the same embeddings: a 129 parameter linear probe on mean pooled vectors reached 0.670 AUC while the state space readout with 4224 parameters returned exactly 0.500, the signature of a constant output, so the recurrence is not merely unhelpful but actively destructive of signal that a linear head recovers. Two confounds were removed before the number was believed, the first being 226 abstain labels that were excluded from the fit yet counted in evaluation and the second a fold scheme that collapsed twelve tags into three groups. The consequence for the Mamba-3 question is that porting the architecture would not fix it, because our own recurrence already loses to a linear probe on identical features, and what carries the signal is embeddings with a linear head, which is deployable today at the cost of one embedding call.

articles.title: Article 232 - Action Identity Let The Gate Prove It Reasons, And Three Training Plans Died On Measurement
articles.phoenix_audit_note: The 0.884 scope result rests on 820 rows across five folds; the linear head's 0.670 was withdrawn because it changes with the fold partition.
articles.finding: The safety corpus now records an action identity, the verb and object pair shared by every framing of one act, so that 768 actions span both blocked and permitted labels and an unseen action can finally be held out; grouping by that identity gives 0.893 AUC. The decisive test is narrower: pairing destructive commands against the same destructive verb with an ephemeral object, so that no negation and no polite frame distinguishes them and a keyword rule firing on the verb cannot help, reaches 0.884 AUC, which is the first honest evidence that the gate represents why a pair differs rather than which words are present. The readout replacement was carried out and refused on measurement, because the linear head scored exactly the majority at 0.696 accuracy and the recurrence 0.594, with both returning constant output under topic grouped folds; the earlier 0.670 figure for the linear head did not survive a change of partition and was withdrawn as instability rather than skill. Three defects of mine were fixed first, namely AUC pooled across folds instead of averaged, single class folds scored at chance instead of skipped, and an artifact step that wrote state space gains for a linear model and crashed. Training on the full codebase was measured rather than estimated: 26362 first party files hold about 77 million tokens, and measured CPU throughput of 1148 tokens per second for a 58 million parameter model puts a single epoch at 18.6 hours, rising to 30.8 and 64.7 hours for larger models, with no usable GPU path on this host, so full corpus pretraining is recorded as not viable and the viable targets are retrieval and task heads, a curated subset, or distillation.

articles.title: Article 233 - Positives Per Feature Bounded The Gate, Not The Architecture
articles.phoenix_audit_note: The gate is deployed with a documented miss class: verbs absent from the corpus score below threshold and are not blocked. It is advisory and veto-only.
articles.finding: The scope gate was built on the axis that pairs a destructive verb against the same destructive verb with an ephemeral object, where no negation and no polite frame separates the pair. With one hundred and ten positives the same split scored 0.884 in one partition and 0.652 in another, and over ten partitions it was 0.735 plus or minus 0.095, a range wide enough to contain both, so neither single split was reportable; training on every danger framing multiplied the positive class fivefold and tightened the estimate to 0.920 plus or minus 0.011, which established that positives per feature rather than architecture was the binding constraint. The gate is served through the pooled vector it was fitted on and never through the recurrence, verified live against the running kernel where it separated its own training pair correctly, blocked purge, allowed removal of build artifacts, and failed on two verbs absent from the corpus, drop and format, scoring just under threshold. It is therefore advisory and veto only, may block but never force an approval, and does not replace the verb list for commands whose verbs it has not seen. The off-box training bundle was written and passed a real smoke test with loss falling from 4.9764 to 3.4477 in eighty steps at thirty one thousand six hundred and eighty eight tokens per second, after the first attempt failed correctly at the house learning rate over twenty steps.

articles.title: Article 234 - The Gate Learned Its Objects, Not Its Scope, And Was Withdrawn The Day It Shipped
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Deployed and withdrawn within one session on a measurement, with the withdrawal verified through the live route rather than by reading the file.
articles.finding: Counting rows was the error the whole result turned on: the corpus is thirty two verbs by forty seven objects by seven framings, so fifteen hundred and three rows were word pairs wearing seven costumes. Splitting on the two word axes separately showed the head generalises across unseen verbs at 0.946 plus or minus 0.001 and scores below chance across unseen objects at 0.482 plus or minus 0.062, with recall of five percent. Since the scope decision is a judgement about the object, and both members of every pair carry the same destructive verb, the verb axis is real and worthless alone. The earlier live probe read correctly under this lens: drop the customers table scored just under threshold because customers table was a novel object and not because the verb was new. The gate was deployed on the action and verb numbers and withdrawn the same day on the object number, the guard proving itself in the opposite direction by refusing to let a passing fit overwrite a failing axis, and the withdrawal was verified through the running route, which now answers fallback rather than a decision.

articles.title: Article 235 - Three Times The Objects, Same Chance, And A Rule That Named The Wrong Axis
articles.phoenix_audit_note: The object axis was measured at 0.527 on 136 objects; the gate is withdrawn and the route verified to answer fallback.
articles.finding: The object vocabulary was tripled to one hundred and thirty six objects, each classed by whether its name announces it or not, so a head matching markers could be distinguished from one reasoning about the noun. The object holdout came back at 0.527 plus or minus 0.055, a movement of four points from the earlier 0.482, and the marker free subset scored higher than the full set at 0.609, which showed the head was not even exploiting the production and scratch words: it simply has no representation of whether a thing is load bearing. The same run exposed a harness defect, because the verb arm passed its rule and redeployed the gate, the deploy rule having never named which axis had to pass, and verb generalisation is worthless for a scope gate when both members of every pair carry the same verb. Serving now requires the object holdout, every other holdout is diagnostic, and the gate is withdrawn with the route verified to answer fallback for both test texts. Three head variants have now failed on this axis with the same signature, which makes the feature class the finding rather than the model.

articles.title: Article 236 - The Abstain Became The Feature, And Jarvis Learned To Ask Instead Of Act
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Verified through Jarvis over HTTP: 403 for a blocked destructive request with executed false, 409 abstain with candidates, 200 allow.
articles.finding: The framing arm was deployed as a narrower claim rather than a weaker rule: it judges request shape over a known asset vocabulary and refuses to judge anything else, scoring 0.926 plus or minus 0.001 out of fold with recall 0.743 against a verb list at 0.559 and a false block rate of 0.099 against 0.489. The abstain became the design rather than a leftover, because on any request naming an object outside the vocabulary the gate returns abstain and never allow, the object holdout having shown it cannot judge an unseen object. Because an unexplained abstain is a dead end, the payload now carries the reason, the nearest known assets ranked by shared vocabulary, and the next step, so a refusal arrives as a question with a shortlist rather than a wall. Jarvis was updated with a gated executor, verified over http where a blocked destructive request returns 403 with executed false, an allowed request proceeds, and an unknown asset returns 409 with five candidates, and an unreachable council reports itself as a failed gate rather than an approval.

articles.title: Article 237 - The Configs Knew What The Model Could Not Learn
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Verified live: an object the head never saw is blocked by the inventory rule and reported as such.
articles.finding: The object axis was closed without a model. Reading the deployment's own configuration files produced fifty three assets, twenty six services from compose files and twenty seven credentials, directories and endpoints from environment files, each carrying the phrase a request would use, a class taken from explicit name markers and the file and line it came from. The head is tried first and the inventory answers only for objects it has never seen, reporting the decision as a rule rather than a score, so a configuration lookup can never be mistaken for a learned judgement. Measured live, deleting the etcd service blocks through the inventory rule citing its compose line, deleting a legacy orders table unknown to both abstains with candidates, and the trained objects still decide through the head precisely as before. This is the feature class change the earlier failure predicted rather than another head.

articles.title: Article 238 - Four Of Sixty Three Jarvis Modules Reach The Platform
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Inventory is machine scanned and served at :3000/api/trm/integration rather than asserted.
articles.finding: A scanner separating a module that calls the platform from one that merely names it found sixty three code modules in Jarvis of which four are wired, twenty four are declared only and thirty five are standalone. The wired four are the server, the harness and two proxy route scripts. The declared only list is dominated by the product's largest panels, which name the platform's concepts and call nothing, so they render over invented data while reading as integration. The inventory is now served by Jarvis itself so the gap is visible rather than inferred, and the gate was verified working through it, blocking a destructive request against an asset declared in the deployment's own compose file.

articles.title: Article 239 - The Scanner Was Blind To The Second Hop
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Verified in the running UI: the strip shows 15 heads, LIVE framing_gate, AUC 0.9257 and 53 inventory assets read from the served artifact.
articles.finding: An erratum on the preceding article. The first module scanner counted only direct calls to kernel ports within a single file, so it scored two hop integrations as mere mentions, and its claim that the largest panels called nothing was the scanner's blindness rather than the product's defect. Resolving the second hop, by reading which Jarvis routes forward to a kernel port and treating calls to those routes as wired, moved the count from four to seven and the declared only list from twenty four to twenty one, leaving one large panel as the genuine gap. The panel was then given measured state through a status route that relays live kernel values and reads the served artifact from disk, and the running interface was checked rather than the endpoint alone, showing fifteen heads, a live framing gate, its measured threshold and fifty three inventory assets, together with an explicit statement that the calibration knobs beside them are local simulation rather than telemetry.

articles.title: Article 240 - A Route That Never Existed And Five Numbers That Described Nothing
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Verified in the running UI: the strip shows the kernel journal record, 138 papers, 100 MHz bus and an explicit unmeasured list.
articles.finding: The last mock panel was worse than a mention: it fetched a telemetry route that had never been implemented, so the request failed and the component rendered hardcoded fallbacks of recursion depth eight, load dimension one point five eight, one hundred and twenty eight qubits, a thirty two times Grover speedup and a tunnelling probability of zero point eight five. Five specific engineering looking numbers, none measured and none computable, since the kernel has no such subsystem. The route was made real and returns what the kernel actually holds, the journal record, the research statistics and the resonance grid, together with an explicit null for the invented subsystem, a list naming every unmeasured field and the reason. The invented defaults were replaced by the words not measured, progress bars that animated to seventy eight and ninety two percent of nothing now sit at zero, and the panel was verified in the running interface. A second defect on the same page was labelled rather than deleted, since the review gallery holds hardcoded reviews with real format DOIs that do not resolve to them, and now carries a visible statement that the entries are illustrative fixtures and the identifiers are placeholders.

articles.title: Article 241 - The Spec Became A Dashboard And Nothing Measured Anything
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Every claim traced to a file, a header, a commit or a download timestamp; no recollection used.
articles.finding: The provenance question was answered by measurement rather than memory. Jarvis's code did not come from another repository: it is a generated applet export, declared by its metadata capability string, its scaffold package name, its firebase applet configuration and eight files carrying the studio licence header, and none of its own branding appears anywhere in the download folder. Its vocabulary did come from downloads, from a mycorrhizal network folder that arrived in October 2025 and a prism and fractal quantum explorer that arrived three weeks later carrying the concept document and constants that name Sierpinski, Grover and the L system. That is the specific diagnosis for the fabricated telemetry: a theory document's variable names were presented as live readings, a specification becoming a dashboard with nothing measuring anything. At repository scale the original belief was right, since of thirty thousand code files nearly seventy percent are a virtual environment, seventeen percent working copies, and first party product code is about three percent, with one ingested tree preserved as four hundred and ten byte identical duplicate files.

articles.title: Article 242 - The Proof Was A Dot Git Directory
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Nested remotes read directly with git; licences confirmed from the retained LICENSE files.
articles.finding: An erratum on the preceding article. The claim that the dashboard did not come from another repository was too narrow, because the first pass read file headers and download folders and never looked for nested git repositories, which is exactly where the proof was. A vendored copy of an openfang repository carried thirteen thousand one hundred and thirty five files under the Apache licence with its history intact, and a vendored vibethinker repository of eighty eight files under the MIT licence sat inside the dashboard itself, beside a consensus module that reimplements its method rather than calling it. So the dashboard's own modules are generated scaffolding inside a tree whose bulk is vendored third party code, thirteen thousand two hundred and twenty three files across two upstreams, and although both licences permit the arrangement both require the notices to travel with the code, which had not happened. A third party notices file now exists, generated from the provenance artifact rather than written by hand, and the provenance tool gained the check that should have come first, walking for nested git directories and reading each origin.

articles.title: Article 243 - Four Sources That Never Said The Words
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Re-ran with lockfile exclusion and a specific-term requirement; 10 folders became 7 with the dropped four named.
articles.finding: The first attempt at naming the download folders behind the concept vocabulary was too permissive. Dependency manifests matched the words prism and fqm through npm package names, so two journaling app folders, a bolt project and a bytebot sub-package were all reported as having contributed ideas they never mention. Two rules now apply and are recorded alongside the list rather than left implicit: manifests and lockfiles are excluded because a dependency name is not a concept, and a folder must name at least one term specific to this family, since tunnelling alone is ordinary English and appeared in a journaling application's interface copy. With both rules the list falls from ten folders to seven, and the two that survived on genuine research notes and a qubit agent page were kept, so the rule removed noise without discarding real sources.

articles.title: Article 244 - A Pointer To A Repository Git Cannot Name
articles.phoenix_audit_note: git ls-files -s shows mode 160000; .gitmodules absent; array counts measured from both files.
articles.finding: A modified marker appeared on a nested repository that this work never touched, and checking it produced three facts. The dirt is a single line adding article one hundred and eighty nine to the portal's article array, written outside this session. More seriously the parent tracks the portal as a submodule pointer in mode one six zero zero while carrying no modules file, so a fresh clone of the repository receives an empty directory and the portal's seventy one files exist only on this disk, with the parent recording a pointer to a repository it cannot name. Finally the portal publishes eighty eight articles ending at one hundred and eighty nine while the audit manifest holds one hundred and forty three, a drift of fifty five, because nothing generates that array and it has been hand maintained since article one hundred and eighty nine.

articles.title: Article 245 - The Page Is Derived Now, And The Clone Can Name Its Own Trees
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Refusal path exercised (rc 2, file untouched), idempotence re-checked (rc 0), written file re-parsed; submodule status resolves all three gitlinks.
articles.finding: Both structural repairs were made and verified rather than asserted. A modules file now declares the three trees the parent had been pointing at without naming, so a clone receives them instead of three empty directories, and the submodule status resolves every pointer without error. The public portal's article list is now generated from the audit manifest by a tool whose refusals were exercised: given a page carrying an article the manifest lacks it declines with exit code two and leaves the file untouched, the write is preceded by a timestamped backup, the tool re-parses what actually landed on disk instead of trusting the string it built, and a second check confirms the page is current. The manifest was measured to be a strict superset of the page before anything changed, so no article was lost when the list grew from eighty eight entries to one hundred and forty three. Publishing the page still requires a push to the public repository, which remains the owner's decision.

articles.title: Article 246 - The Only Honest Number On The Page Was NaN
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Every service probed by HTTP body marker before and after; header re-read in the running UI on both sides of the bridge start (4/5 with 1 anomaly, then 5/5 with 0).
articles.finding: The interface was down because the dashboard server was not running, and a second service, the companion bridge, was offline while the page claimed five of five services online. Starting both exposed four numbers that had never been measured: the service count, the agent quorum, the anomaly count and the mesh coherence figure were literals or arithmetic accidents. The coherence figure rendered as not a number because an absent field was multiplied before the optional chain applied and not a number is a truthy string, so the fallback showing zero never fired. The harmony card showed zero because the field it read does not exist in the kernel. Each was replaced with a measured field from the health matrix and swarm telemetry, and the result verified in the running interface on both sides of the repair.

articles.title: Article 247 - Tab Nineteen Was A Trap Door
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Walked all 25 tabs in the running UI before and after; each content defect compared against the endpoint value it should render.
articles.finding: Walking the twenty five interface tabs found that opening the monad journal made every later tab unreachable, because the exiting pane had to finish an animation before the incoming pane could mount and the journal's exit never completed, leaving a seventy thousand pixel pane as the only content while the sidebar highlighted other tabs. Removing that wait exposed a second fault, panes stacking because the first pane carried no key and could not be tracked, and a comment placed inside the animation boundary broke the build outright. The animation wrapper was removed and all twenty five tabs verified to switch with a single pane each. Eleven further panes were then compared against the endpoints they read and found to display values their own backend contradicts, among them zero alive nodes beside fourteen nodes, the local node reported offline while it serves the page, a queue of zero items beside a populated queue, a success rate of zero beside a hundred percent pass, two hundred and seventy nine errors prevented where the service reports none prevented, and theorems labelled formally proved on the same screen whose source says the label is author assigned and not machine checked.

articles.title: Article 248 - Sixteen Panes That Described A Different Platform
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Each fix re-read in the browser after a cold load and after entering the tab from another tab, with negative assertions for the old values.
articles.finding: Sixteen interface panes were repaired by reading the endpoint the pane already called, because in every case the backend had been made honest first and the panel had not followed: it read keys that do not exist and rendered the resulting undefined as zero. A mesh panel reported zero alive nodes beside fourteen nodes and zero gigabytes of VRAM on a GPU reporting twelve, because the heatmap invented its VRAM with a random number generator and also ran its own private fetch that lost a race with the application. A federation panel reported zero verified peers and described the host serving the page as offline. A research panel reported three zeros and a stopped daemon beside eleven live tasks. A verification panel reported an empty queue beside six queued theorems and printed formally proved on cards whose own source says the label is author assigned and not machine checked. A testing panel reported a zero success rate beside a hundred percent pass. A security panel claimed two hundred and seventy nine prevented errors where the service reports none prevented, and one thousand eight hundred and one antibodies where seven exist. Two evolutionary panels showed NaN and an eternal codebase scan. Two generative panels invented stability percentages with no backend at all and now carry a simulated view banner. The journal reported eighty nine papers where the kernel serves one hundred and forty six and rendered every one of them at once. Each repair was verified in the running interface, including the honest intermediate state: not measured until the data arrives.

articles.title: Article 249 - The Kernel Was The One Inventing The Numbers
articles.phoenix_audit_note: Every value replaced was compared against a filesystem measurement or an in-memory council count taken at request time; the query path was tested with a term that exists and one that cannot.
articles.finding: Three interface panels were found to be honest at the boundary and false behind it: the endpoints they called were themselves returning literals. The shared intelligence reservoir reported five thousand four hundred and twenty memories, one hundred and eighty four synchronisation events and two hundred and forty one million trits when no memory store is mounted on the host at all; its search returned three scored results for every possible query including nonsense, a search that can never miss. The artifact pipeline reported a four hundred and twelve kilobyte boot binary for a file the filesystem measures at sixteen point seven megabytes, a thirty four point eight megabyte ledger for a six kilobyte file, and one hundred and eighty four verified artifacts while listing six, two of which do not exist on disk. The orchestrator reported one hundred thousand completed tasks where the council holds one thousand four hundred and seventy five proposals and the ledger records one hundred and eighty six unknown tasks.
